title: From Drift to Coherence: Stabilizing Beliefs in LLMs
claim: Predictive beliefs drift substantially in early resampling steps, violating coherence, but conditioning on seed answers removes that early drift.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared axes, left-to-right, shaded std bands
description: Two side-by-side line plots share the same axes. The x-axis is sequence length n, from 1 to 30. The y-axis is the expected predictive probability E[θ_n(x_Q)], from 0 to 0.6. Each plot has five colored lines for answer options A–E (blue, orange, green, red, purple). Each line has a translucent shaded band of ±1 standard deviation, and the legend sits in the top right. Gray dashed gridlines are drawn. In panel (a), 'Without seed answers', the curves move a lot over the first few steps. The bands are wide and overlapping, and the lines slowly converge. The red D line stays flat at zero. In panel (b), 'With seed answers', the curves are much flatter and stable from the start, and the bands are narrower. Large italic captions under each panel label the two conditions. The eye goes first to the orange and purple curves, which show the contrast in drift.
caption: Analysis of martingale property violation in prompted predictive resampling. We instructed LLAMA-3.1-8B to generate a sequence of answers on the CSQA question. Solid lines indicate the mean across independent sample paths, and shaded regions represent ±1 standard deviation. (a) A significant drift during the early generated sequences was observed, indicating the martingale violation. (b) Conditioning on a prefix of 5 random i.i.d. sequences effectively mitigates the drift.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often hypothesized to perform implicit Bayesian inference, yet a key coherence condition, the martingale property of predictive beliefs, has been shown to fail in controlled synthetic in-context learning settings. We revisit this question in a more typical usage regime: generic multiple-choice question answering. Exploiting the discrete answer space, we compute exact predictive distributions and study belief dynamics induced by autoregressive answer resampling. We introduce prompted predictive resampling (PPR), where an LLM generates a sequence of answers to the same question. Empirically, PPR reveals early-stage belief drift, indicating martingale violations. However, after sufficient resampling steps, the belief process self-stabilizes and converges to a coherent predictive distribution. Based on this observation, we further propose (i) a seed-answer prompting strategy to accelerate stabilization, and (ii) a self-consistency loss that amortizes early-stage drift into the model via fine-tuning. Experiments on multiple-choice QA benchmarks show that our methods substantially reduce belief drift and improve predictive coherence without sacrificing accuracy.
